title: Sleep deprivation: a night without sleep
description: Not an illness but a state everyone knows: a night without sleep. The episode follows the brain the next day while trying to pay attention and to learn something new. Areas that hold attention become less active, while the thalamus, a relay at the centre of the brain, becomes more active. The comparison is with the same kind of task after a normal night's sleep.
caveat: The attention findings come from a pooled analysis of 11 studies, 185 people in all, using different tasks; individual studies had reported both increases and decreases, and the pooled result is what was consistent across them. The memory finding comes from one study. These are effects of one full night without sleep in healthy volunteers; ongoing partial sleep loss may differ. Activity is measured while doing a task, so it is not activity at rest.

phases.name: A night awake
phases.caption: A full night passes without sleep. The brain is not scanned during the night itself in these studies.

phases.name: Trying to pay attention
phases.caption: The next day, during an attention task, areas that hold attention are less active than after normal sleep: the parietal attention areas, the insula, the right prefrontal cortex and the medial frontal cortex. The thalamus is more active, which the authors suggest may reflect a complex interaction between sleepiness and the effort of doing the task.

order.rationale: The scans are taken after the night awake, by design; the night itself is not measured.

phases.name: Trying to learn
phases.caption: Learning something new, the hippocampus, which forms new memories, is less active than after sleep, and less is remembered later. The attention findings are not carried over to this separate task.

order.rationale: The memory finding comes from a separate study. Placing it after the attention task is a way of presenting both.

phases.name: After sleep
phases.caption: Recovery after sleep was not studied in the sources read; the return to normal drawn here is an assumption.

order.rationale: No source read scanned people after recovery sleep. The return to rest is assumed.

regions.explanation: The intraparietal sulcus, a key attention area, was less active on both sides after a night without sleep, in a pooled analysis. It lies at the upper edge of the inferior parietal cortex, which is drawn.

citations.authors: Ma N, Dinges DF, Basner M, Rao H
citations.title: How acute total sleep loss affects the attending brain: a meta-analysis of neuroimaging studies.
citations.quote: The meta-analysis revealed significantly reduced brain activation in multiple regions following sleep deprivation compared to rested wakefulness, including bilateral intraparietal sulcus, bilateral insula, right prefrontal cortex, medial frontal cortex, and right parahippocampal gyrus.
